title: Sequence Diagram Essentials
explanation: Sequence diagrams show how objects or components interact over time by depicting the order of messages exchanged between them. They are invaluable for documenting API interactions, authentication flows, and service-to-service communication patterns. This module covers UML sequence diagram notation and best practices for architecture documentation.

annotations.explanation: A vertical dashed line representing the existence of a participant (actor or system component) over time.
A solid arrow with a filled arrowhead representing a call that waits for a response.
A dashed arrow showing the response returned to the caller.

walkthrough.instruction: Identify the participants (actors and system components) and place them as lifelines across the top of the diagram.
Draw the messages between participants in chronological order from top to bottom.
Add return messages, activation bars, and any alternative or loop fragments as needed.

exercises.scenario: Model the authentication flow for a government service where a user logs in via GOV.UK One Login, the service validates the token with the identity provider, and returns the user's session.
hints: Include User, Web Application, and GOV.UK One Login as participants
Show the redirect to the identity provider
Include the token validation and session creation steps

commonMistakes.description: Not showing return messages for synchronous calls
commonMistakes.incorrectExample: Drawing a request arrow from Service A to Service B without a corresponding return arrow
commonMistakes.correctedExample: Always pair synchronous request arrows with dashed return arrows showing the response
commonMistakes.explanation: Omitting return messages makes it unclear whether a call is synchronous or asynchronous (fire-and-forget), which can lead to incorrect assumptions about system behaviour and error handling.
